findings.claim: The 6Rs framework (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Reclaim, Repair and Rethink) - repeated in the glossary, the 6-mark mark scheme and a flashcard.
findings.truth: This specification names the six Rs as rethink, reuse, recycle, repair, reduce and refuse. Reclaim is not one of them and Refuse was missing, so a student taught this list would name a wrong R and miss a taught one.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/design-and-technology-C600QS.md line 544: 'The SIX R's of sustainability; rethink, reuse, recycle, repair, reduce and refuse.'

findings.claim: KC 4: 'The 6Rs sustainability framework includes Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Reclaim, Repair and _____.' correct = 3 (Rethink), with 'Refuse' offered as a wrong option.
findings.truth: Refuse is one of the six Rs on this specification, so the question marked a true answer wrong. Stem, distractor and answer index all corrected.
findings.evidence: spec line 544; answer-key recheck against the corrected list.

findings.claim: 'Answers that only cite one property will not reach the higher mark bands at Eduqas.'
findings.truth: House rule: an Eduqas/WJEC lesson must never name the board in student-facing prose. Neutral phrasing only.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings; project house rule.

findings.claim: 'Heat treatment processes ... are generally not used for mild steel (too little carbon to respond significantly)'.
findings.truth: Only hardening and tempering fail on mild steel. Annealing, normalising and case hardening are all routinely used on it - the same lesson says annealing restores ductility to work-hardened metal and that case hardening is specifically for mild steel, so the text contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: spec line 2002-2004 (heat treatment of ferrous metals: annealing, hardening, tempering and case hardening); internal contradiction with bullets n28 and n32.

findings.claim: 'A hacksaw blade should have at least two teeth in contact with thin material at all times'.
findings.truth: The blade-selection rule is a minimum of three teeth in the material.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Hacksaw: 'The blade chosen is based on the thickness of the material being cut, with a minimum of three teeth in the material.'

findings.claim: 'an argon/CO&sub2; mix makes it MAG welding'.
findings.truth: &sub2; is not an HTML entity, so the live page printed the literal string 'CO&sub2;'. The subscript must be CO<sub>2</sub>.
findings.evidence: HTML named character reference list; raw field inspection.

findings.claim: Q2: 'Name two stock forms in which aluminium sheet metal is commercially supplied.'
findings.truth: Sheet is itself a stock form, so the stem ruled out its own mark scheme, which credits bar, rod, tube and angle. The stem should ask about aluminium, not aluminium sheet metal.
findings.evidence: spec line 2134-2139 (stock forms: rod, strip, sheet, tube, angle, channel); mark scheme in the same question.

findings.claim: 'Gold and lead are the most malleable metals'.
findings.truth: Gold and silver head the malleability order; lead sits well below aluminium and copper. The claim is not mark-affecting because lead is genuinely malleable, but the superlative is loose.
findings.evidence: standard malleability order (gold, silver, aluminium, copper, tin, lead, zinc, iron).

findings.claim: 'copper has the highest electrical conductivity of commonly used metals'.
findings.truth: Silver is the best electrical conductor of all metals, and this specification names silver as a non-ferrous metal to study. The hedge 'commonly used' carries the claim, so no edit, but it is fragile.
findings.evidence: spec line 2009 (silver is on the non-ferrous list).

findings.claim: 'arc welding steel reaches approximately 3,500 degrees Celsius at the arc'.
findings.truth: Welding arc column temperatures are normally quoted well above this. No settled figure was found inside the fetch budget (the Wikipedia arc-welding article gives no temperature), so the value is left alone.
findings.evidence: WebFetch of Wikipedia, Arc welding - no temperature stated; WebSearch budget exhausted.

findings.claim: 'around 86% of steel used in the UK is recycled'.
findings.truth: Unsourced. UK steel recycling is normally reported per sector (construction, vehicles, packaging), not as one national rate. The neighbouring figures (74% energy saving for recycled steel, 5% for recycled aluminium) are standard and correct.
findings.evidence: no primary source reachable within the fetch budget.

findings.claim: 'Pop rivets ... are widely used in aircraft skins' immediately before 'solid rivets (used in structural steelwork and older aircraft)'.
findings.truth: Production aircraft skins are mostly solid-riveted; blind rivets are chosen where only one side can be reached. The two sentences pull against each other, but neither is examinable detail on this specification.
findings.evidence: spec line 2284 lists riveting without this level of detail.

summary: Twelve findings across five lessons: seven fixed, five recorded as notes. The unit taught the wrong sixth R (Reclaim instead of Refuse), which reached the glossary, a knowledge check that marked the true answer wrong, a mark scheme and a flashcard. One lesson named the board in prose; one denied that mild steel can be heat treated at all; one printed a broken HTML entity for carbon dioxide.
